source_text: οἵδε μὲν οἱ χρόνοι τῶν παρ’ Ἕλλησι πρεσβυτάτων σοφῶν τε καὶ φιλοσόφων. ὡς δὲ οἱ πλεῖστοι αὐτῶν βάρβαροι τὸ γένος καὶ παρὰ βαρβάροις παιδευθέντες, τί δεῖ καὶ λέγειν, εἰ γε Τυρρηνὸς ἢ Τύριος ὁ Πυθαγόρας ἐδείκνυτο, Ἀντισθένης δὲ Φρὺξ ἦν καὶ Ὀρφεὺς Οδρύσης ἢ Θρᾷξ; Ὅμηρον γὰρ οἱ πλεῖστοι Αἰγύπτιον φαίνουσιν. Θαλῆς δὲ Φοῖνιξ ὢν τὸ γένος καὶ τοῖς Αἰγυπτίων προφήταις συμβεβληκέναι εἴρηται, καθάπερ καὶ ὁ Πυθαγόρας αὐτοῖς γε τούτοις, δἰ οὓς καὶ περιετέμετο, ἵνα δὴ καὶ εἰς τὰ ἄδυτα κατελθὼν τὴν μυστικὴν παρ’ Αἰγυπτίων ἐκμάθοι φιλοσοφίαν, Χαλδαίων τε καὶ Μάγων τοῖς ἀρίστοις συνεγένετο καὶ τὴν ἐκκλησίαν τὴν νῦν οὕτω καλουμένην τὸ παρ’ αὐτῷ ὁμακοεῖον αἰνίττεται. Πλάτων δὲ οὐκ ἀρνεῖται τὰ κάλλιστα εἰς φιλοσοφίαν παρὰ τῶν βαρβάρων ἐμπορεύεσθαι εἴς τε Αἴγυπτον ἀφικέσθαι ὁμολογεῖ. δύνασθαι γοῦν ἐν τῷ Φαίδωνί φησι πανταχόθεν τὸν φιλόσοφον ὠφελεῖσθαι γράφων· πολλὴ μὲν ἡ Ἑλλάς, ἔφη, ὦ Κέβης, ἦ δ’ ὅς, ἐν ᾗ εἰσι πάμπαν ἀγαθοὶ ἄνδρες, πολλὰ δὲ καὶ τὰ τῶν βαρβάρων γένη. οὕτως οἴεται ὁ Πλάτων καὶ βαρβάρων φιλοσόφους τινὰς εἶναι, ὁ δὲ Ἐπίκουρος ἔμπαλιν ὑπολαμβάνει μόνους φιλοσοφῆσαι Ἕλληνας δύνασθαι. ἔν τε τῷ Συμποσίῳ ἐπαινῶν Πλάτων τοὺς βαρβάρους ὡς διαφερόντως ἀσκήσαντας † μόνους ἀληθῶς φησι καὶ ἄλλοι ἄλλοθι πολλαχοῦ καὶ ἐν Ἕλλησι καὶ βαρβάροις, ὧν καὶ ἱερὰ πολλὰ ἤδη γέγονε διὰ τοὺς τοιούτους παῖδας. δῆλοι δέ εἰσιν οἱ βάρβαροι διαφερόντως τιμήσαντες τοὺς αὐτῶν νομοθέτας τε καὶ διδασκάλους θεοὺς προσειπόντες. ψυχὰς γὰρ ἀγαθὰς κατὰ Πλάτωνα καταλιπούσας τὸν ὑπερουράνιον τόπον ὑπομεῖναι ἐλθεῖν εἰς τόνδε τὸν τάρταρον καὶ σῶμα ἀναλαβούσας τῶν ἐν γενέσει κακῶν ἁπάντων μετασχεῖν ὑπολαμβάνουσι, κηδομένας τοῦ τῶν ἀνθρώπων γένους, αἳ νόμους τε ἔθεσαν καὶ φιλοσοφίαν ἐκήρυξαν, οὗ μεῖζον ἀγαθὸν τῷ τῶν ἀνθρώπων γένει οὔτ’ ἦλθέν ποτε ἐκ θεῶν οὔτ’ ἀφίξεται. καὶ μοι δοκοῦσιν αἰσθόμενοι τῆς μεγάλης εὐποιίας τῆς διὰ τῶν σοφῶν σεβασθῆναί τε τοὺς ἄνδρας καὶ δημοσίᾳ φιλοσοφῆσαι. Βραχμᾶνές τε σύμπαντες καὶ Ὀδρύσαι καὶ Γέται καὶ τὸ τῶν Αἰγυπτίων γένος ἐθεολόγησαν ἀκριβῶς τὰ ἐκείνων, Χαλδαῖοί τε καὶ Ἀράβιοι οἱ κληθέντες εὐδαίμονες καὶ ὅσοι γε τὴν Παλαιστίνην κατῴκησαν καὶ τοῦ Περσικοῦ γένους οὐ τὸ ἐλάχιστον μέρος καὶ ἄλλα πρὸς τούτοις γένη μυρία. ὁ δὲ Πλάτων δῆλον ὡς σεμνύνων αἰεὶ τοὺς βαρβάρους εὑρίσκεται, μεμνημένος αὐτοῦ τε καὶ Πυθαγόρου τὰ πλεῖστα καὶ γενναιότατα τῶν δογμάτων ἐν βαρβάροις μαθόντος. διὰ τοῦτο καὶ γένη βαρβάρων εἶπεν, γένη φιλοσόφων ἀνδρῶν βαρβάρων γινώσκων, ἔν τε τῷ Φαίδρῳ τὸν Αἰγύπτιον βασιλέα καὶ τοῦ Θωὺθ ἡμῖν σοφώτερον δείκνυσιν, ὅντινα Ἑρμῆν οἶδεν ὄντα. ἀλλὰ κἀν τῷ Χαρμίδῃ Θρᾷκάς τινας ἐπιστάμενος φαίνεται, οἳ λέγονται ἀθανατίζειν τὴν ψυχήν.
pass_a_gloss: These indeed are the times of the oldest wise men and philosophers among the Greeks. But since most of them are of barbarian race and were educated among barbarians, what need is there to say, if Pythagoras was shown to be a Tyrrhenian or a Tyrian, and Antisthenes was a Phrygian and Orpheus was an Odrysian or a Thracian? For most people think Homer was an Egyptian. And Thales, being a Phoenician by race, is said to have associated with the prophets of the Egyptians, just like Pythagoras with these same people, through whom he also was circumcised, so that he might go down into the innermost sanctum and learn the mystical philosophy of the Egyptians. And he came to be with the best of the Chaldeans and Magi, and he hints at the church now so called, which was the gathering place with him. Plato does not deny that the most beautiful things in philosophy were imported from the barbarians, and he agrees that he arrived in Egypt. For in the Phaedo he says that the philosopher can be benefited from everywhere, writing: 'Greece is a large place, he said, O Cebes, and there are altogether good men in it, and there are many things among the barbarian races.' Thus Plato thinks that there are some barbarian philosophers, but Epicurus holds the opposite view, that only Greeks can philosophize. And in the Symposium, Plato praises the barbarians as having excelled in their practice, saying they alone truly philosophize, and there are others elsewhere, both among Greeks and barbarians, for whom many sacred things have already been done through such children. The barbarians are clearly those who have especially honored their own lawgivers and teachers, calling them gods. For they think that good souls, having left the heavenly place, come into this underworld and, having taken on a body, share in all the evils of generation, being concerned for the human race, which has been given laws and philosophy by them, which is the greatest good that has come or will come from the gods to the human race. And it seems to me that, perceiving the great benefit that has been given through the wise men, they have revered these men and philosophized publicly. The Brahmans and the Odrysians and the Getae and the Egyptian race have all spoken accurately about these things, and the Chaldeans and the Arabs who are called happy, and as many as have inhabited Palestine, and not the smallest part of the Persian race, and many other races besides these. And Plato is clearly found to always honor the barbarians, remembering that he and Pythagoras learned most and the most noble of their doctrines among the barbarians. Therefore, he also said that there are races of barbarian philosophers, knowing that there are races of barbarian men who are philosophers. And in the Phaedrus, he shows the Egyptian king to be wiser than us, whom he knows to be Hermes. But also in the Charmides, he appears to know some Thracians who are said to make the soul immortal.
pass_b_english: These are the dates for the earliest Greek sages and philosophers. Yet since most of them were foreigners by birth and received their education among foreign peoples, there is little need to add more examples: Pythagoras is reported to have been Tyrrhenian or Tyrian, Antisthenes was Phrygian, and Orpheus was either Odrysian or Thracian. Most authorities even claim Homer was Egyptian. Thales, a Phoenician by birth, is said to have associated with the Egyptian prophets, just as Pythagoras did with those same men; through them he was circumcised so that he could enter the innermost sanctuaries and learn the Egyptians’ mystical philosophy. He also consorted with the foremost Chaldeans and Magi, and he alludes to the assembly now called the church, which served as his own gathering place. Plato does not deny that philosophy’s finest gifts were imported from foreign peoples, and he acknowledges his own journey to Egypt. In the Phaedo he writes that the philosopher can profit from every quarter: ‘Greece is wide, Cebes, and in it there are thoroughly good men; there are also many foreign nations.’ Thus Plato believes that some foreigners are philosophers, whereas Epicurus holds the opposite view—that only Greeks can philosophize. In the Symposium Plato praises the barbarians for their surpassing practice, saying they alone truly philosophize, and he notes that others, both among Greeks and barbarians, have already had many sacred rites performed for them because of such men. The barbarians plainly honored their own lawgivers and teachers by calling them gods. For they believed that good souls, leaving the heavenly realm, descended into this underworld, took on bodies, and shared in all the evils of mortal life out of concern for the human race—giving them laws and proclaiming philosophy, the greatest good that has ever come or will come from the gods to humanity. It seems to me that, sensing the magnitude of this benefit conferred through the wise, they revered those men and practiced philosophy publicly. The Brahmans, the Odrysians, the Getae, and the Egyptian people have all spoken precisely about these matters, as have the Chaldeans and the Arabs called happy, all who dwelt in Palestine, no small portion of the Persian people, and countless other nations besides. Plato is clearly found to honor the barbarians continually, recalling that he and Pythagoras learned their most numerous and noblest doctrines among them. For this reason he spoke of ‘barbarian races,’ knowing that there are races of barbarian men who are philosophers. In the Phaedrus he presents the Egyptian king as wiser than ourselves, identifying him as Hermes. And in the Charmides he shows knowledge of certain Thracians who are said to make the soul immortal.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Greek text, including the complex descriptions of the soul's descent and the various ethnic groups mentioned. The distinction between Plato's view and Epicurus's view is preserved. All scripture/philosophical references (Phaedo, Symposium, Phaedrus, Charmides) are correctly identified and matched to the text.
